### Why the pier logger reads warmer than the offshore buoy

Hello, divers, tidepoolers, and data-curious neighbors,

Several people have asked why my pier temperature logger consistently reads warmer than the offshore buoy—and whether the logger is simply faulty. The short answer is that both instruments can be working correctly while measuring different water.

Here are the numbers:

|  | Pier logger | Offshore buoy |
|---|---|---|
| October mean temperature | **15.9°C** | **14.1°C** |
| October difference | **About 1.8°C warmer at the pier** | |
| Winter difference | **About 0.4°C warmer at the pier** | |
| Location | Piling at 3 m depth, about 150 m from shore | About 25 km offshore, sensor just below the surface in deep water |

The gap is real, local oceanography, not an instrument error. Shallow nearshore water warms in the sun, particularly on bright afternoons. Our sheltered bay also has some protection from the upwelling that brings cold deep water to the surface offshore. As solar heating weakens and conditions change in winter, the two records move closer together.

One reader sent me a genuinely helpful screenshot overlaying the buoy and pier data. It shows the gap tracking sunny afternoons—exactly the pattern you would expect if local heating were contributing to it.

For those wondering how I check the instrument: it logs every 10 minutes, and I retrieve and download it every six weeks, replacing the battery annually. Its calibration check uses two baths—an ice bath and a room-temperature bath—against a laboratory reference thermometer. At the last check, in September 2026, the logger’s offset was **+0.12°C**, well inside specification and far too small to explain a 1.8°C difference.

I also check the less glamorous possibilities. In August, I pulled it up carrying a barnacle colony and a decorator crab that had taken up residence on the housing. I scraped everything off; the readings did not change.

The buoy and logger answer different questions. The buoy is useful for offshore conditions; if you are diving the breakwater, the pier measurement is generally the more relevant number.

If you would like the raw CSV files to examine or plot yourself, email me and I’ll happily send them.

—**[Name]**  
Marine biologist, Monterey, California
